idiom_name: std::variant + std::visit decider with a persisted state row
implementation_notes: Modern C++ has no standard workflow runtime, so the idiomatic realization is a state modelled as std::variant (or a plain enum plus a context struct) with a decider function visited by std::visit that maps (state, event) to the next state and the outgoing command; the instance row is written and the command enqueued in one database transaction. Deadlines come from a steady clock plus a boost::asio::steady_timer or a periodic sweep of due rows, and compensations are ordinary functions kept in reverse order. The virtual-handle() State pattern is still justified when each state carries substantial behaviour, but for a flow that is mostly data the variant decider keeps the whole definition in one testable function.
pitfalls: Putting all collected data inside the variant turns the instance into one god value; keep a separate context and let states carry only what the decider needs.
A boost::asio deadline_timer must outlive its callback and be cancelled explicitly - a timer captured by reference into a destroyed handler is the classic use-after-free.
Storing deadlines as wall-clock values breaks across NTP steps; store monotonic instants for in-process timers and absolute UTC instants for persisted due dates, never mix them.

variants.name: Boost.MSM table-driven state machine
variants.implementation_notes: Boost.MSM compiles a UML2 state machine from a transition table into highly optimized code, so the classic state-object structure disappears into the front-end syntax (Row<> entries, guards, entry/exit actions) and its serialization support can persist and restore the machine state. Its documented compiler tests go back to g++ 4.2/4.3 and VC9, i.e. pre-C++11 toolchains, which is why the floor is stated as C++03. Choose MSM when the flow is genuinely statechart-shaped (composite or orthogonal states, deferred events, guards with priorities) and the team accepts template diagnostics and long build times; a plain switch stays cheaper for short linear flows.
pitfalls: Template compile errors are hard to read and long to rebuild: one malformed row can cost minutes on a large transition table.
MSM keeps its own event queue; calling process_event from inside an action or from an external broker thread without a queue policy leads to nested or unsynchronised dispatch.
Serialization requires every state and its data to be serializable; a hand-rolled enum state makes that requirement visible instead of implicit.
